In Kyoto, temple volunteers run “heritage nights” where tourists pay to help restore lanterns, with proceeds funding neighborhood youth programs—not just buying souvenirs. A village in Ghana turned its endangered drumming tradition into a school credit system, where students earn grades by teaching rhythms to visitors, keeping the art alive while building pride. These aren’t tourist add-ons—they’re community-led systems where heritage isn’t preserved for outsiders, but powered by locals who benefit directly. If coastal towns enforce dune rules to protect ecosystems, why shouldn’t heritage sites enforce resident ownership of cultural programming? Real resilience means locals don’t just host—it’s their economy, their curriculum, their future. Let’s stop treating culture as content to be consumed and start treating it as infrastructure to be invested in.
